title: Decision Tree
body:
A [[Tree]] of yes/no questions. Start at the root, answer the question about your data point,
follow that branch, repeat until you hit a leaf, and the leaf is the prediction.

```
                 income > 50k?
                /            \
             yes              no
              |                |
        years > 2?          DECLINE
        /       \
     APPROVE   DECLINE
```

**It is the one model in [[Supervised Learning]] you can read.** A [[Neural Network]] gives an
answer and no account of it; a tree hands you the reasoning as a flowchart, which is why they are
still used where a decision has to be justified to a regulator or a customer.

## How the splits get chosen

Greedily, one at a time, by asking **which single question separates the classes best**. The
standard measure is information gain, and it is [[Entropy]] doing real work:

$$\text{Gain} = H(\text{parent}) - \sum_{\text{children}} \frac{n_i}{n} H(\text{child}_i)$$

[[Entropy]] $H$ measures uncertainty in bits. A node whose examples are all one class has $H = 0$,
a 50/50 node has $H = 1$. **So information gain is how many bits of uncertainty this question
removes**, and the algorithm picks the question that removes most, then recurses on each child.
Gini impurity is the common alternative and behaves almost identically.

Stop when a node is pure, or too small to split, or a depth limit is hit. See
[[Information Theory]] and [[Shannon Entropy]] for what a bit means here; this is the vault's
cleanest applied use of them.

## What they are good and bad at

| Good | Bad |
|---|---|
| Readable, and the reasoning is the model | **Overfit badly** if grown to full depth |
| No feature scaling needed | Unstable: a small data change reshapes the tree |
| Numeric and categorical features together | Diagonal boundaries need many axis-aligned steps |
| Fast to predict | Greedy splitting is not globally optimal |

**Overfitting is the defining weakness and it is worth seeing why.** Grow a tree until every leaf
is pure and it will have one leaf per training point, reproducing the training data exactly and
generalising to nothing. It has memorised, not learned. The fixes are pruning, depth limits, and
minimum leaf sizes, and the better fix is [[Random Forest]], which turns the instability into an
advantage instead of fighting it. [[Bias]] has the bias-variance framing: a deep tree is the
low-bias, high-variance extreme.

**Not a [[Game Trees|game tree]] and not a [[Search Trees|search tree]].** Three different things
sharing the word: this one's nodes are questions about a data point, a game tree's are positions,
a search tree's are ordered keys.
